title: CRePE: Curved Ray Expectation Positional Encoding for Unified-Camera-Controlled Video Generation
claim: One model generates coherent video under extreme non-pinhole cameras while exposing the internal geometry it uses for control.
layout: 2 stacked rows, camera icon left, frames over geometry heatmaps, time arrow
description: The figure has two stacked rows, one for a wide-angle camera and one for a fisheye camera. On the left of each row is a gray field-of-view fan diagram with a camera icon. It is labeled with the lens type, xFoV (160° or 180°) and a distortion parameter ξ. Next to it is a small colored camera-trajectory ribbon and a text caption prompt, with key scene phrases in blue. A time arrow runs above each strip. Below the arrow are four generated frames: a night market street and a motorcycle dealership interior. Both show wide-lens distortion. Under each frame strip is a matching row of predicted-geometry heatmaps in a blue-to-red colormap. The heatmaps show nearby people as warm blobs. The eye goes first to the vivid photographic frames, then to the heatmaps.
caption: Fisheye and wide-lens camera-conditioned video generation. Each row shows a video generated by CRePE under a non-pinhole camera trajectory, alongside the internal geometry map the model estimates and utilizes during generation --- the per-token expected radial distance along its viewing ray, integrated into the rotary phasor at each denoising step. Top: wide-angle camera trajectory with the corresponding generated frames and geometry map. Bottom: fisheye trajectory with its generated frames and geometry map. The geometry map is internal to CRePE rather than an external input: it is a latent positional variable decoded from the geometry head, not the output of a depth decoder or a metric depth estimate.
abstract: Camera-conditioned video generation requires positional encoding that remains reliable under changes in camera motion, lens configuration, and scene structure. However, existing attention-level camera encodings either provide ray-only camera signals or rely on pinhole camera geometry, limiting their applicability to general camera control under the Unified Camera Model, including wide-angle and fisheye lenses. To address this limitation, we propose Curved Ray Expectation Positional Encoding (CRePE). CRePE represents each image token as a depth-aware positional distribution along its source ray, providing a Unified Camera Model-compatible positional encoding that naturally captures the curved-ray geometry of wide-angle and fisheye cameras. CRePE is implemented through a Geometric Attention Adapter added to frozen video DiTs, injecting token-wise scene-distance information into selected attention layers and stabilizing it with pseudo supervision from a monocular geometry foundation model. This design leads to more stable camera control with competitive video quality in camera-conditioned video generation under the Unified Camera Model, and the resulting model transfers zero-shot to real fisheye and diverse pinhole videos. Controlled positional-encoding ablations show improvements over a RayRoPE-style endpoint approximation, demonstrating the effectiveness of curved-ray-aware positional encoding, particularly for non-pinhole cameras. Furthermore, by extending the same positional-encoding pathway to external geometry control through Radial MixForcing, CRePE supports external radial-map control for scene-geometry-conditioned generation and source-video motion transfer beyond camera control. Project page: https://crepe-neurips2026.github.io/; code: https://github.com/jinotter3/CRePE.
